investigator.value: Tom Bissell, a magazine journalist and essayist who arranges an interview with the masked vigilante known as the Avenger in a remote wooded location
investigator.quote: Six months ago I wrote an essay for this magazine...I had not, of course, interviewed the Avenger for my essay.

suspect_architecture.value: No traditional suspect cast. The Avenger is the sole quasi-criminal figure; the architecture is binary — anonymous vigilante vs. the city's criminal underclass — with legal ambiguity replacing a suspect spread. The NYPD, mayor, and press function as institutional antagonists rather than suspects.
suspect_architecture.quote: Was he a polite Bernhard Goetz? A human Superman? A witty sociopath? A professional headline seeker? A nut? A saint?

red_herring.value: The Avenger's public persona and rehearsed sloganeering ('I am a most unique man'; 'I am the force that will make civilization civil') misdirect press and public toward a mythic superhero archetype, concealing a wounded, physically fragile, morally ambivalent man who is frequently injured and uncertain of his own purpose.
red_herring.quote: the man whom in our sacred unease we fantasized as a harsh sentinel, an incorruptible guardian, sounded more like a slurring crackpot

clue_fairness.value: Not applicable as a traditional mystery. However, the narrator withholds from the reader the Avenger's stated reason for the meeting ('which will have to wait'), denying both narrator and reader the resolution — a deliberate structural withholding rather than fair-clue placement.
clue_fairness.quote: I asked you here for one reason. Which will have to wait, because someone is coming.

social_world.value: New York City's layered power structure: NYPD and mayoral authority vs. extralegal vigilantism; celebrity media economy vs. anonymous virtue; the press as arbiter of public legitimacy. Class is implicit — the Avenger terrorises poor, circumstantially criminal youth while being celebrated by institutions.
social_world.quote: I essentially terrorize poor kids who had shitty situations to begin with. Am I happy about that? I am not.

alibi.value: Not applicable in a classical sense. The Avenger's anonymity functions as a perpetual, structural alibi — no one can place him anywhere because no one knows who he is. His trip-wire surveillance device and planned escape routes are described as pre-emptive alibi mechanics.
alibi.quote: If anyone happens along, I'll be out of sight in twenty seconds, give or take. And you won't be able to follow me.

reveal_mechanic.value: The reveal is psychological and incomplete: the Avenger demonstrates his vulnerability (dentures, broken ribs, Kevlar, financial modesty) to deconstruct his own myth, and the interview structure itself is the mechanism — but the central revelation (why he summoned the narrator) is never delivered, leaving the mechanic deliberately suspended.
reveal_mechanic.quote: More than half of my teeth have been knocked out. Mostly dentures... I get hurt all the time.

media_and_audience.value: Central structural element. The Post and Times frame competing narratives (populist hero vs. civic menace); YouTube virality shapes public perception; the mayor grants unprecedented legal status under media pressure; academic dissertations and the World Superhero Registry show institutionalised myth-making. The narrator's own essay is part of this media architecture.
media_and_audience.quote: Our news cycles will have a different algorithm now, synced to the actions of a man no one can find, no one knows.

investigator_wound.value: The narrator's brother died trying to intervene against a stronger party victimising a weaker one — the exact impulse the Avenger embodies. The narrator studied martial arts after the death, then abandoned it. His anti-Avenger essay is a rationalised displacement of grief, guilt, and fear of his own weakness.
investigator_wound.quote: I worried you would inspire people to step into situations they have no business stepping into... I didn't like feeling weak.
